text.p: Union Bank of Switzerland (UBS) had a good start to 1997 and is confident of a satisfactory group result for year as a whole, UBS chief executive Mathis Cabiallavetta said.

"The results for the first quarter are not yet available in their entirity, but it is already clear that we have had a very good start to 1997," Cabiallavetta said in a speech to the annual shareholders' meeting.
"January and February were exceptionally good months, athough March was weaker," he added.
Cabiallavetta said it would be rash to predict "record earnings" for 1997 on the basis of first quarter figures and conditions on financial markets could change abruptly.

UBS in February reported a 348 million franc ($236.7 million) 1996 group net loss. The loss was due to one-time charges totalling 4.4 million francs to cover credit risks linked to its domestic loan portfolio.
Separately, Cabiallavetta also renewed the UBS pledge to remain a universal bank rather than narrowing its focus.

But he also stressed that management still planned to expand the asset management side and believed an acquisition was likely, perhaps in the U.S., in order to establish a significant presence in the world's biggest asset management market.

"Particularly in our activities outside Switzerland, we believe a further expansion will bring significant benefits, and there is some likelihood that we will do this via acquisition," Cabiallavetta said at the meeting.

UBS' new structure, in place since the start of the year, consists of private banking and institutional asset management, trading, international and domestic corporate finance and Swiss retail business.
Cabiallavetta noted that asset management was the strongest earnings driver.
The shareholders meeting was expected to produce few fireworks since it was the first since 1994 not attended by shareholder activist and Swiss financier Martin Ebner.
Ebner is the most prominent critic of the bank. His BZ Bank investment trust is the biggest shareholder in UBS.
Ebner has pressed UBS for years to shed its less profitable businesses and become exclusively an asset manager in order to boost shareholder value.
The battle heated up in 1994 when UBS decided to change its share structure in a move that had the effect of dramatically reducing BZ's voting power.
But Ebner, who has been supportive of Cabiallavetta's management style since he took the chief executive post last April, had said earlier that he would not attend the meeting.
Asked before the shareholders' meeting whether his absence was a vote of confidence on Cabiallavetta's leadership, Ebner told Reuters, "Yes, in the sense of 'benefit of the doubt'".
UBS executives also explained the motives behind joining with Switzerland's other big banks to create a Holocaust memorial fund.

The three banks in February were the first to donate money for a humanitarian fund for Holocaust survivors that the Swiss government then formally created using the cash and another 165 million francs from private companies and the central bank.

UBS chairman Robert Studer told shareholders there were business reasons as well as humanitarian motives in donating 100 million Swiss francs together with rivals Credit Suisse Group and Swiss Bank Corp.
"Our position there (the U.S.) and our reputation, on which banking relationships are largely based, are at stake and are being increasingly called into question," Studer said.

The memorial fund and a broader government plan to create a seven billion Swiss franc foundation to help the world's poor and persecuted came about in the past two months under mounting pressure led by U.S.-based Jewish groups and U.S. politicians.

At the crux of the controversy are Jewish claims that Swiss banks withheld accounts left by Holocaust victims and that Switzerland generally profited cynically from its status as a neutral financial centre during World War Two. ($ = 1.47 Swiss Francs)
